explanations.explanation: This feature detects and signals standardized header text, including copyright and legal boilerplate (such as file headers, licensing notices, and court case citations), that typically appear at the top of source code files or legal documents.

It seems the feature “lights up” whenever the model processes tokens that aren’t ordinary language words but rather serve as special‐formatting or “placeholder” markers—often nonstandard or mis‐encoded characters that appear amid text boundaries (whether in legal citations, foreign language passages, or markup elements) and which signal a change or disruption in the usual linguistic flow.

It marks the “tail‐piece” of a multi‐token word—that is, it lights up on subword endings (whether parts of names, dates/numbers, or other compounds) that signal a completed unit. In other words, the feature detects terminal fragments (or “suffixes”) that play a role in forming proper names, numeric expressions, URLs, etc., thereby cueing the model’s next‐token predictions based on completed lexical units.

This feature identifies and encodes formal, structured citation and metadata language—such as legal case names, docket numbers, publication details, and other standardized reference formats—that appear in official documents and news headlines.

It’s a signal for a distinctive sub‐token that almost always appears as the “continuation” piece in a multi‐part, technical or identifier-like term. In other words, the feature is activated on fragments (often prefixed or split with special markers like “**”) that join together pieces of compound words (e.g. in code names, file names, version hashes, and other technical strings) so that the model treats them differently than ordinary full-word tokens.

It appears that this feature “lights up” on the little connective or modifier tokens that set up comparisons, intensifications, or evaluative relationships in a sentence—for example, in phrases like “as … as,” “so …”, “such …”, “all,” or “than.” In short, the model has a specialized sensitivity for the function‐words that signal comparative, intensifying, or relational constructions in language.

explanations.explanation: This feature detects and encodes structured legal citation and document header patterns—identifying tokens that signal case numbers, docket and document identifiers (like “Case:”, “Document:”, “Page:”, “Date Filed:”), and associated court metadata—in legal texts.

It appears that the feature “fires” on segments that mark a sub‐morphemic or compound boundary—i.e. it detects word parts (often in names, technical terms, or inflected forms) whose ending is sensitive to morphological or orthographic variation. In other words, this feature encodes patterns of internal word segmentation and influences which variant ending (or “tail”) is predicted next.

This feature fires when the model is processing strongly formatted, “metadata‐style” content—tokens that are part of structured, often numeric or identifier‐rich strings (like ISBNs, time codes, version numbers, code dumps, URLs, etc.). In short, it signals that the text is in a technical or data‐formatted register and helps steer prediction for those “field‐boundary” tokens.

It detects the standard legal boilerplate (the Apache License header) and, in particular, the exception clause phrasing (“except … in compliance with the License”) that marks a restricted usage clause in copyright/license texts.

It appears that this feature “lights up” when the model is processing a subword fragment that is meant to complete a larger, morphologically or orthographically compound unit. In other words, it tracks when a token is the tail‐end (or “glue” element) of a word or name—often seen in legal, technical, or multi‐lingual text—helping the model decide that the next token will finish or extend a previously started morpheme.

It appears that this feature has learned to “flag” subword fragments—pieces of a multi‐token word (often in proper names, technical terms, or compound phrases) that are not stand-alone and which cue the model to continue with the expected completion.

It appears this feature is capturing a “pair‐oriented” or compound‐token concept—in particular, it detects when a token is part of a paired or hyphenated expression whose “other half” is a semantic or syntactic counterpart (for example, width versus height, sci‑fi components, or compound names like X‑Men). In short, the feature represents the model’s learned signal for compound or bipolar relationships between tokens, so that when it’s “removed” the next token shifts to its counterpart (its contrapositive) in the learned pair.

It’s a feature that signals a non‐generic, “structured” context—in other words, it marks that the model is in a specialized (often templated or promotional/boilerplate) context so that instead of defaulting to a bland, common continuation like “the,” it produces tokens (such as template delimiters or context‐specific phrasing) appropriate to that particular format.
It detects standard boilerplate legal header text—copyright and license disclaimers and notice blocks—commonly found at the top of source code files.
